When a Juvenile Institution Moves, Who Runs Its Network?

By Furaihan Kamyl Arnazaye · 2025 · 6 min read
Key takeaways
  • LPKA Kelas II Jakarta moved from Salemba to Cinere in January 2020. The move changed how its partner network was governed, from a network brokered by Kanwil to one led by LPKA itself.
  • No authority was formally transferred. The shift followed a change in how partners perceived LPKA's legitimacy.
  • Built from 1,789 Instagram posts and 11 interviews, the network grew from 41 to 189 organizations. Density fell from 0.133 to 0.032, and degree centralization rose from 0.806 to 0.989.
  • Judged against the conditions of a lead organization, the move was effective on trust, goal consensus, and network-level competence.
  • The mismatch is size. LPKA now leads more partners, of more types, than a lead organization handles well.
  • The recommendation is fewer partners, chosen by clear criteria and grouped into thematic working groups.

On 21 January 2020, LPKA Kelas II Jakarta moved out of a building it shared with an adult prison in Salemba and into its own facility in Cinere. LPKA is Lembaga Pembinaan Khusus Anak, Indonesia's special correctional institution for children. The move was meant to give the children a place built for them. My thesis asked what the move did to the organizations around them.

Those organizations matter because LPKA cannot run its programs alone. According to Direktorat Jenderal Pemasyarakatan, the number of children in LPKA across Indonesia grew from 823 in 2020 to 1,444 in 2024, a 75.4% increase in five years. Budgets, facilities, and staff did not grow at the same pace. The gap is filled by partners. Schools, NGOs, religious groups, the police, the civil registry, and ministries each run part of the program. If the relocation disrupted that network, the children would feel it long before anyone measured it.

Turning a relocation into a comparison

The research question was simple. How did the effectiveness of LPKA's network governance change after the relocation? A relocation is useful to a researcher because it is a single event with a date. Everything before 21 January 2020 is Salemba. Everything after is Cinere. That split gives a before and an after without anyone having to design an intervention.

The harder part was the data. No list of LPKA's partners existed. The official website published too few activities to build a representative network, which was the main weakness of the earlier PKM study I wrote about in PIMNAS. So I scraped Instagram and kept only posts that showed an in-person activity between organizations. Two organizations appearing in the same activity became a tie. Each organization was coded by level, from national agencies to international organizations, and by the period in which it appeared.

Network metrics describe structure. They do not explain it. I interviewed eleven informants from seven organizations, including Ditjenpas, the police, Disdukcapil Jakarta, Bapas Jakarta Selatan, Ruang Damai, and PKBM Hasanah, and observed activities in Cinere on 4 July 2024. The interviews were my check on whether the numbers meant what I thought they meant.

Not every tie means the same thing. A joint raid, a graduation ceremony, and a counseling program all create a tie, so I classified every interaction into three types. Coordination on operations and governance was the most frequent, followed by ceremonies. Programs for the children themselves were the least frequent of the three.

The analytical choice that shaped everything else was the benchmark. A dense, tightly connected network sounds healthy. Whether it is healthy depends on who is supposed to run it. Provan and Kenis (2008) describe three forms of network governance, and each one works under different conditions of trust, number of participants, goal consensus, and the competence the network needs.

FormTrustParticipantsGoal consensusCompetence needed
Shared governanceHigh densityFewHighLow
Lead organizationCinereLow density, highly centralizedModerateModerately lowModerate
NAOSalembaModerate density, NAO monitored by membersModerate to manyModerately highHigh

So the order of the analysis mattered. I first identified which form LPKA's network had in each period. Then I judged each period against the conditions of its own form, translating each condition into network metrics. Trust, for example, was read through density, centralization, and the average strength of ties.

What changed after the move

The network became much larger and much more centralized. It also became thinner. Organizations had more partners on average, 6.042 against 5.317, but interacted with each of them less often.

In Salemba, the network had 41 organizations and a density of 0.133. The center was shared by three actors: LPKA, the regional office of the Ministry of Law and Human Rights (Kanwil Kemenkumham DKI Jakarta), and Lapas Salemba. Kanwil acted as the broker. Only 7 of Kanwil's 247 weighted ties in Salemba ran directly to LPKA. The rest connected Kanwil to everyone else. The interviews said the same thing. Disdukcapil Jakarta described coordinating through Kanwil as its entry point. Bapas Jakarta Selatan copied its assessments of the children to Kanwil. That is an NAO.

In Cinere, the network grew to 189 organizations. Degree centralization rose from 0.806 to 0.989, close to the maximum of 1. LPKA's own weighted degree more than doubled, from 326 to 743. Of Kanwil's 356 weighted ties, 169 now ran to LPKA. Partners described LPKA setting the direction. Ruang Damai said LPKA's leadership gave direction on its program, including parenting sessions for the children's parents. PKBM Hasanah said its curriculum was designed on LPKA's input. That is a lead organization.

No authority was formally transferred from Kanwil to LPKA. What changed was how network members perceived LPKA's legitimacy after the relocation. The police still coordinated through Kanwil or Bapas in both periods, so part of the old structure stayed in place.

Effective, with one mismatch

Judged against the conditions of a lead organization, the relocation was effective on three of the four conditions. Trust, goal consensus, and network-level competence all fit the new form. The Expected column shows the direction each metric should move if the new form works.

Several results look backwards at first. Density fell by roughly three quarters, and that counts as effective. A lead organization is expected to run a sparse network in which most ties pass through itself. The same logic applies to the lower average tie strength.

The mismatch is size. A lead organization carries the coordination cost of every member on its own, so it works best with a moderate number of participants. LPKA's network grew from 41 to 189 organizations. Adjusted for the longer Cinere period, it still nearly doubled, from 0.056 to 0.106 organizations per day of data. Heterogeneity rose from 76.51% to 85.25%.

The growth was uneven. Correctional institutions went from none to 20. Courts, prosecutors, and police went from 4 to 34. Adjusted for time, provincial agencies and private partners appeared less often in Cinere than in Salemba.

Key findingLPKA took on the role of a lead organization without the capacity to lead a network this large and this varied.

The recommendation follows from that finding. LPKA needs fewer partners, chosen more deliberately. Ditjenpas can set a framework for how LPKAs manage their networks, with criteria for selecting partners, a classification of which interactions take priority, and a simpler format for documenting cooperation. LPKA can then group its partners into thematic working groups by program focus, each with a small set of organizations whose resources complement each other.

The recommendations are also written up as a four-page policy brief, in Indonesian, with my supervisor Dr. Lina Miftahul Jannah. The brief adds the risks of each option and how to reduce them.

The data has limits that anyone relying on it should know. Instagram only captures what LPKA and Lapas Salemba chose to publish, so unpublished interactions are missing. I also did not collect data from the children themselves. The study measures how the network is governed. It does not measure whether the children are better off. Answering that needs the children's perspective.

The question I would leave LPKA with is which of its 189 partners the children actually need.
